plan.topic: Survodutide (glucagon + GLP-1 dual agonist) in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes: SYNCHRONIZE-2 Phase 3 (NEJM, 1 Oct 2026, n=752, 76 weeks): up to 13.1% weight loss (highest-dose arm) vs 3.1% on placebo; A1C down up to 1.21 points
plan.angle: Working title (≤100 chars): 'Survodutide in Type 2 Diabetes: 9.8% vs 3.9% Placebo at 76 Weeks. Why Did Investors Shrug?' Alternative if 13.1% is kept: 'Survodutide's 13.1% in T2D: What It Means (and Why Shares Fell)'. Only use this version if the first 10s immediately says '13.1% is the top dose if people stayed on treatment. Counting everyone, the paper reports 9.8% vs 3.9% on placebo.' First 10s: adults with obesity/overweight AND type 2 diabetes, 76 weeks, both estimands with their own placebo figures (13.1% vs 3.1% if staying on treatment; −9.8% vs −3.9% for everyone randomised, 6.0 mg), and 'investigational, not approved as of Oct 2026'. Give A1C per arm from NEJM (−0.9 / −0.8 vs −0.2 points from 7.4%; add mmol/mol), and mention the 1.21 figure only as the release's 'if stayed on treatment' number. Disappointment: 'Zealand Pharma shares fell about 11% on 1 Oct. Analysts cited tolerability and competition.' This is an investor view, not a clinical verdict. Give tolerability per arm from NEJM: GI AEs 72.8% / 77.7% vs 38.6%, plus vomiting and stopping due to side effects for each arm vs placebo. Explain why weight loss is lower in T2D in every major trial of this class (STEP 2, SURMOUNT-2, TRIUMPH-2), with each trial's estimand, duration and dose labelled as a separate trial with no head-to-head. Liver: 'liver-fat reduction was seen in an earlier substudy; MASH outcome trials are still running.' Nothing changes for people on approved medicines. Close with: 'It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.'
plan.working_title: Survodutide Lost 13.1% (Top Dose) vs 3.1% Placebo in T2D. Why Did It 'Disappoint'?
plan.why: A brand-new NEJM Phase 3 trial with 'disappointment' headlines, almost no creator explainers yet, and enough depth for 10+ minutes. A named-drug headline decoder is our best-performing title formula. | fact-check: The topic is real and on-pillar. SYNCHRONIZE-2 was published in NEJM (Survodutide Once Weekly in Adults with Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes, https://www.nejm.org/doi/10.1056/NEJMoa2607219) with a Boehringer release dated 1 Oct 2026. But the topic line mixes up estimands. 13.1% vs 3.1% and 'A1C down up to 1.21' are the press release's EFFICACY estimand (if people stayed on treatment). The NEJM abstract reports week-76 weight change of −8.2% (3.6 mg), −9.8% (6.0 mg) and −3.9% (placebo). A1C changed by −0.9 (3.6 mg), −0.8 (6.0 mg) and −0.2 points (placebo) from a baseline of 7.4%, so the best A1C result was NOT in the highest-dose arm. Our rule is to use the paper's number, not the press release's 'up to'. n also needs checking: the release says 755, the topic says 752. Use the NEJM randomised and analysed n. Discontinuation is inconsistent across sources: the release says 18% vs 1.2% on placebo, while news coverage (Fierce, Bloomberg) cites 26% stopping after an adverse event and 39% vomiting. Copy the AE-discontinuation and vomiting rates per arm from the NEJM tables only. GI AEs of 72.8% / 77.7% vs 38.6% are confirmed. The 'disappointment' framing is verifiable: Zealand shares fell about 11–12% on 1 Oct, and analysts pointed to tolerability and competitiveness (Bloomberg, Fierce Biotech). Attribute it to investors and analysts, and don't use the word 'markets' broadly. Sponsor: Boehringer Ingelheim (survodutide licensed from Zealand). Say 'developed by Boehringer Ingelheim with Zealand Pharma' unless NEJM lists Zealand as a funder. Comparators: TRIUMPH-2 is now peer-reviewed (Lancet, 29 Sep 2026, retatrutide −11.9/−16.8/−18.8% vs −5.1% at 80 wk), so it can be included. SURMOUNT-2 and STEP 2 are fine too. Label every figure with its estimand, duration and population, and state that there is no head-to-head comparison. Liver: SYNCHRONIZE-2 itself didn't establish a MASH benefit. Liver-fat data come from a SYNCHRONIZE-1 substudy and from Phase 2 MASH work, and Phase 3 MASH outcomes are still ongoing. Label it that way. Survodutide is investigational and not approved as of Oct 2026 (FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation is not approval).

package.description:
Survodutide weight loss in type 2 diabetes plus overweight or obesity: on the higher trial dose, this investigational glucagon + GLP-1 dual agonist lowered body weight by 9.8% vs 3.9% on placebo at 76 weeks, counting everyone randomized.

Quick answer: In Phase 3 SYNCHRONIZE-2 (NEJM, Oct 2026, n=752), the 13.1% vs 3.1% figure is the top dose counting only people who stayed on treatment. A1C (baseline 7.4%, 57 mmol/mol) fell 0.9 points (lower dose) and 0.8 (higher dose) vs 0.2 on placebo, counting everyone; Boehringer's stayed-on-treatment figure was up to 1.21 vs 0.03. Gut side effects: 72.8% and 77.7% vs 38.6% on placebo. Boehringer reported about 18% stopped because of gut side effects vs 1.2% on placebo. Zealand Pharma shares fell about 11% on Oct 1, Fierce Biotech reported. A falling share price is not a failed trial.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Survodutide is investigational and not approved as of Oct 2026. It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
1. Boehringer Ingelheim SYNCHRONIZE-2 release: https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/10/01/3372564/0/en/boehringer-ingelheim-s-survodutide-achieves-up-to-13-1-weight-loss-in-new-phase-iii-trial-alongside-significant-improvements-in-glycemic-control-in-people-with-obesity-and-type-2-d.html
2. Fierce Biotech, Zealand shares: https://www.fiercebiotech.com/biotech/zealand-pharma-slides-boehringer-partnered-obesity-drug-underwhelms-again-phase-3
3. Healio, survodutide in T2D: https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinology/20261001/survodutide-induces-impressive-amount-of-weight-loss-in-type-2-diabetes-and-obesity
4. Healio, retatrutide TRIUMPH-2: https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinology/20260930/retatrutide-confers-substantial-weight-loss-for-adults-with-obesity-type-2-diabetes
package.pinned_comment: On the higher dose, survodutide lowered weight 9.8% vs 3.9% on placebo over 76 weeks (counting everyone) in adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity, and A1C fell more than on placebo. But about 3 in 4 reported gut side effects (vs about 2 in 5 on placebo), and Zealand Pharma's shares fell about 11% that day. Which number would you check first in a headline: the "up to" figure or the count of everyone? Survodutide is investigational and not approved as of Oct 2026. Educational only, not medical advice. It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.working_title: Survodutide Weight Loss in Type 2 Diabetes: 9.8% vs 3.9% Placebo at 76 Weeks. Why Did Shares Fall?
script.hook_pattern: Counterintuitive claim: a good trial result and a falling share price on the same day. Within 10 seconds the hook names the dose and gives both ways of counting, each with its own placebo figure. It also plants an open loop ('the one question that tells a 13.1% from a 9.8%') that pays off in the final chapter.

scenes.narration: On its higher trial dose, survodutide helped adults with type 2 diabetes lose 9.8% of their body weight over 76 weeks, versus 3.9% on placebo. The same day, Zealand Pharma's shares fell about 11%.
scenes.retention_device: Pattern interrupt: a positive result next to a falling share price opens an instant 'why?' gap

scenes.narration: You may also see a bigger number: 13.1%. That's the top dose, counting only people who stayed on treatment, versus 3.1% on placebo. The 9.8% counts everyone who was randomized.
scenes.retention_device: The second number arrives straight away, so viewers sense a puzzle worth solving

scenes.narration: That's in about 750 adults with overweight or obesity plus type 2 diabetes. And survodutide is investigational: as of October 2026, it's not an approved medicine.
scenes.retention_device: Stakes and scope set early, so the viewer knows exactly who this applies to

scenes.narration: So which number is real? Both. And by the end, you'll know the one question that tells them apart in any GLP-1 headline you'll ever read.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop planted: the 'one question' pays off in the final chapter

scenes.narration: Along the way: a blood sugar result that runs backwards, a pattern seen across major diabetes trials in this class, and what investors were worried about.
scenes.retention_device: Roadmap of three open loops that carries viewers through the middle sections

scenes.narration: First, what makes survodutide different? Most weight medicines you've heard of, like semaglutide, mimic one gut hormone: GLP-1.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card resets attention with a simple question

scenes.narration: Your gut releases GLP-1 after you eat. It signals fullness to your brain, slows how fast your stomach empties, and helps your pancreas release insulin when blood sugar rises.

items: Helps release insulin when sugar rises

scenes.retention_device: A concrete 'you' explanation lays the groundwork for the twist that follows

scenes.narration: Survodutide mimics GLP-1 too. But it also turns on a second receptor, for a hormone called glucagon. Think of it as one key that opens two locks.
scenes.retention_device: A vivid analogy makes the dual mechanism easy to remember

scenes.narration: And here's where it gets weird. Glucagon's best-known job is to raise blood sugar. So why put it in a drug for people with diabetes?
scenes.retention_device: 'Here's where it gets weird' re-hook with a paradox question

scenes.narration: Because glucagon does more than that. It nudges the liver to burn stored fat, and in early studies it raised the energy the body uses. Much of that evidence comes from animal and early human research.
scenes.retention_device: The paradox is resolved, with an honest caveat about how strong the evidence is

scenes.narration: The GLP-1 half is there to keep blood sugar in check while the glucagon half works on the liver and energy use. At least, that's the design.
scenes.retention_device: 'At least, that's the design' hints the real-world result may differ

scenes.narration: It's developed by Boehringer Ingelheim, which licensed it from a Danish company called Zealand Pharma. Hold on to that second name.
scenes.retention_device: Micro open loop: Zealand returns in the investor chapter

scenes.narration: The trial is called SYNCHRONIZE-2. It was published in the New England Journal of Medicine on October 1, 2026.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter change signals new, concrete evidence

scenes.narration: 752 adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes were randomly assigned to weekly survodutide, at a 3.6 or 6.0 milligram trial dose, or to placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Clear trial-design micro-story

scenes.narration: They were followed for 76 weeks. That's almost a year and a half.
scenes.retention_device: A short, punchy sentence varies the rhythm

scenes.narration: Their average starting A1C, the 2-to-3-month blood sugar average, was 7.4%. That's about 57 mmol/mol. Remember that number. It comes back later.
scenes.retention_device: Explicit 'remember this' open loop, paid off in the blood sugar chapter

scenes.narration: Now, why two weight-loss numbers from one trial? Because trials can ask two different questions.
scenes.retention_device: Returns to the hook's puzzle and starts paying it off

scenes.narration: Question one: what happened to everyone who was randomized, including people who stopped the drug? That's closer to real life, where not everyone keeps going.
scenes.retention_device: Simple framing of the first way of counting

scenes.narration: Question two: what happened if people stayed on treatment as planned? That's usually the bigger number, and it's the one press releases tend to lead with.
scenes.on_screen_text: Q2: Only if they stayed on
scenes.retention_device: An insider tip the viewer can reuse, which builds trust

scenes.narration: Counting everyone, weight fell 8.2% on the lower dose and 9.8% on the higher dose, versus 3.9% on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Concrete numbers with their comparator

scenes.narration: Counting only people who stayed on treatment, Boehringer reported up to 13.1% on the top dose, versus 3.1% on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Top dose vs −3.1% placebo, if stayed on

scenes.retention_device: Side-by-side contrast with the previous stat

scenes.narration: Same trial, same people. The difference is who gets counted. And when the two numbers sit far apart, it's often a hint that many people stopped or missed treatment.
scenes.retention_device: Plants a new loop (why did people stop?) that pays off in the side effect chapter

scenes.narration: Which is exactly where this story is heading. But first, the result that surprised me most.
scenes.retention_device: Mini-cliffhanger before the section change

scenes.narration: Quick question. Which dose do you think lowered blood sugar more, the higher one or the lower one? Most people would guess the higher one.
scenes.retention_device: A direct question makes the viewer commit to a guess

scenes.narration: A1C fell 0.9 points on the lower dose and 0.8 points on the higher dose, versus 0.2 points on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Pays off the viewer's guess with a counterintuitive answer

scenes.narration: In mmol/mol, that's drops of roughly 10, 9 and 2. Both doses lowered A1C more than placebo, but the top dose didn't come out on top.
scenes.retention_device: Units every viewer can use, plus the twist restated

scenes.narration: You might see a 1.21-point A1C drop in headlines, versus 0.03 on placebo. That's the company's figure for people who stayed on treatment, not the paper's count of everyone.

visual.fact: That's the company's stayed-on-treatment figure (vs 0.03 on placebo). Counting everyone, the paper reports −0.9 / −0.8 vs −0.2

scenes.retention_device: Myth-fact correction of a number viewers will see online

scenes.narration: Why would a higher dose not lower A1C more? This trial alone can't say, and a 0.1-point gap may simply be chance.
scenes.retention_device: Honest uncertainty builds credibility before the next clue

scenes.narration: But remember that starting number, 7.4%? At that level, there's less room to fall than in trials where people started higher.

visual.stock_query: ball on low shelf near floor

scenes.retention_device: Pays off the 'remember 7.4%' loop

scenes.narration: In STEP 2, people with type 2 diabetes started around 8.1%, and semaglutide 2.4 milligrams lowered A1C by 1.6 points, versus 0.4 on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: A named-drug comparison keeps it concrete

scenes.narration: In SURMOUNT-2, people started around 8.0%, and tirzepatide lowered it by about 2.1 points, versus 0.5 on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: A second comparator builds the pattern

scenes.narration: Those are separate trials with different people and lengths, and there's no head-to-head. So you can't rank the drugs. But a lower starting A1C generally leaves room for a smaller drop.
scenes.retention_device: The caveat lands as a takeaway, then the section changes

scenes.narration: Now the part analysts focused on: how people felt on it.
scenes.retention_device: Pays off the 'why did people stop?' loop and links it to the investor mystery

scenes.narration: Gut side effects were reported by 72.8% on the lower dose and 77.7% on the higher dose, versus 38.6% on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Big, surprising stat

scenes.narration: That's about 3 in 4 people on survodutide, compared with about 2 in 5 on placebo. Think nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and constipation, the usual pattern for this drug class.
scenes.retention_device: Turns percentages into people the viewer can picture

scenes.narration: Notice that placebo number. Nearly 4 in 10 people reported gut symptoms on a dummy injection. What matters is what the drug adds on top.

visual.stock_query: dummy injection pen with question mark

scenes.retention_device: A counterintuitive detail most coverage skips

scenes.narration: For context, in STEP 2, gut side effects were reported by 63.5% on semaglutide 2.4 milligrams, versus 34.3% on placebo. Again, a separate trial, not a head-to-head.

visual.stat_label: STEP 2 gut side effects vs 34.3% placebo
visual.stock_query: two separate charts side by side

scenes.retention_device: A named comparator gives the viewer a reference point

scenes.narration: And more people stopped. Boehringer reported that about 18% of people on survodutide stopped because of gut side effects, versus 1.2% on placebo. And reports covering the investor reaction focused on how many people stopped.

visual.stat_label: Stopped due to gut side effects, company-reported

scenes.retention_device: Pays off the loop about the gap between the two numbers with the dropout figure and its placebo comparator, and teases the investor chapter

scenes.narration: One warning: reports quoted different stopping rates. Boehringer's 18% counts only gut side effects. Fierce Biotech reported 26% stopping after any side effect, without a placebo figure. Always check which one a headline means, and the per-arm tables in the paper.

items: No placebo figure given for the 26%

scenes.retention_device: Transparency moment that teaches viewers to check the primary source

scenes.narration: So the weight loss was real, but it came with a lot of stomach trouble. And there's a second reason the number looked smaller than people hoped.
scenes.retention_device: New open loop before the section change

scenes.narration: Here's a pattern that rarely makes the headlines. In major trials of this drug class, people with type 2 diabetes lose less weight than people without it.
scenes.retention_device: The promised loop about a pattern across diabetes trials starts paying off

scenes.narration: Semaglutide first. In STEP 1, adults without diabetes who had obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, lost 14.9% over 68 weeks, versus 2.4% on placebo, counting everyone.
scenes.retention_device: Concrete named-drug evidence

scenes.narration: In STEP 2, adults with type 2 diabetes on the same 2.4 milligram dose lost 9.6%, versus 3.4% on placebo, also over 68 weeks.
scenes.retention_device: The contrast makes the pattern visible

scenes.narration: Tirzepatide shows the same pattern. In SURMOUNT-1, in adults without diabetes with a BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with a weight-related condition, the top dose reached 20.9% at 72 weeks, versus 3.1% on placebo, counting everyone.
scenes.retention_device: A second drug repeats the pattern, building conviction

scenes.narration: In SURMOUNT-2, with type 2 diabetes, it was 12.8% and 14.7% on the two doses tested, versus 3.2% on placebo, also at 72 weeks.
scenes.retention_device: A second named pair confirms the pattern

scenes.narration: And in late September 2026, The Lancet published TRIUMPH-2, testing retatrutide, another investigational drug, in adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity.
scenes.retention_device: A brand-new trial adds timeliness

scenes.narration: At 80 weeks, counting everyone randomized, weight fell 11.9%, 16.8% and 18.8% across three doses, versus 5.1% on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: A surprising stat from the newest trial

scenes.narration: Every one of these is a separate trial, with its own length, doses and population. None tested these drugs head-to-head. But the direction is consistent: diabetes trials land lower.
scenes.retention_device: Caveat plus pattern, followed by a 'why?' question

scenes.narration: Why? Researchers have proposed a few explanations. None is fully settled.
scenes.retention_device: A short question line sets up a numbered reveal

scenes.narration: One: when blood sugar runs high, some sugar, and its calories, spills into the urine. As treatment brings sugar down, the body holds on to more of those calories.
scenes.retention_device: Counterintuitive mechanism: better blood sugar can slow weight loss

scenes.narration: Two: in everyday life, many people with type 2 diabetes also take medicines like insulin or sulfonylureas, which tend to promote weight gain. That may also make weight harder to lose.
scenes.retention_device: The numbered list keeps momentum

scenes.narration: Three: people in diabetes trials are often older, with longer-standing metabolic changes that may make weight harder to shift.
scenes.retention_device: Completes the list

scenes.narration: So survodutide's 9.8% belongs next to other diabetes trials, not next to numbers from people without diabetes. But even in that company, investors had a sharper question.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff, then a new loop into the investor chapter

scenes.narration: Which brings us back to that share drop.
scenes.retention_device: The hook's main mystery starts paying off

scenes.narration: On October 1, Zealand Pharma shares fell about 11% in morning trading, Fierce Biotech reported. Analysts pointed to two concerns: tolerability and competition.

visual.stat_label: Zealand Pharma shares, morning of 1 Oct 2026

scenes.retention_device: Stat with clear attribution

scenes.narration: Competition, because this space is crowded. Semaglutide and tirzepatide are already approved, and newer drugs, including pills and triple-hormone medicines like retatrutide, are moving through the pipeline.
scenes.retention_device: Vivid race analogy

scenes.narration: Tolerability, because a drug that most people feel in their gut has to offer something extra to stand out.
scenes.retention_device: Links back to the side effect chapter

scenes.narration: But a falling share price doesn't mean the trial failed. Weight and A1C both fell more than on placebo.

visual.myth: Shares fell, so the trial failed
visual.fact: Weight and A1C fell more than on placebo

scenes.retention_device: Myth attack on the 'disappointment' framing

scenes.narration: A share price is investors' bet on future sales. It's not a clinical verdict on whether a medicine can help patients.
scenes.retention_device: A reframe the viewer can repeat

scenes.narration: And it says nothing about the other reason survodutide exists. Remember that glucagon key, and the liver?
scenes.retention_device: Callback to the early 'two keys' setup opens the liver chapter

scenes.narration: Survodutide's glucagon half was built with the liver in mind.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card for the section that saves the biggest surprise for last

scenes.narration: In a 48-week Phase 2 trial in adults with MASH, a serious form of fatty liver disease with scarring, survodutide improved MASH on biopsy without worsening scarring more often than placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Promising evidence, labelled by trial phase and length

scenes.narration: And in an earlier Phase 3 substudy, from the SYNCHRONIZE-1 trial, Boehringer reported reductions in liver fat.
scenes.retention_device: A second clue, clearly attributed

scenes.narration: But SYNCHRONIZE-2 itself didn't establish a liver benefit. And the Phase 3 MASH outcome trials are still running as of October 2026.
scenes.retention_device: The 'but' turn keeps it honest and opens a forward-looking loop

scenes.narration: Survodutide also has an FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation for MASH. That can speed up development and review. It is not an approval.

visual.fact: It can speed up development and review. It is not an approval

scenes.retention_device: Myth-fact on a commonly misread label

scenes.narration: So the liver may turn out to be where a glucagon-plus-GLP-1 drug earns its place. May. We'll know when those trials report.
scenes.retention_device: Cliffhanger that points to future coverage

scenes.narration: So what does this mean if you live with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity?
scenes.retention_device: Turns the science into a personal question

scenes.narration: If you're on an approved medicine, nothing changes today. Survodutide is still investigational, and it hasn't been compared head-to-head with what you take.
scenes.retention_device: Reassurance eases any anxiety the headlines may have created

scenes.narration: Approved options like semaglutide and tirzepatide have Phase 3 data in people with type 2 diabetes, including the STEP 2 and SURMOUNT-2 trials we just covered.
scenes.retention_device: Callback to earlier sections

scenes.narration: There's no approved survodutide to buy. Anything sold online under that name is not an approved medicine, so please don't go looking for it.
scenes.retention_device: Safety guardrail delivered warmly

scenes.narration: And if gut side effects are what worry you about this whole drug class, that's a great thing to raise with your prescriber, before and during treatment.
scenes.retention_device: Practical action step

scenes.narration: It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
scenes.retention_device: Required prescriber line before the final payoff

scenes.section: How to read any GLP-1 headline
scenes.narration: Now, the payoff I promised: the one question that tells a 13.1% from a 9.8%.
scenes.retention_device: Pays off the main open loop from the hook

scenes.section: How to read any GLP-1 headline
scenes.narration: It's this: counting whom? Everyone who was randomized, or only the people who stayed on treatment?
scenes.retention_device: The reveal, short and memorable

scenes.section: How to read any GLP-1 headline
scenes.narration: Ask it of survodutide, and 13.1% versus 3.1% becomes 9.8% versus 3.9%. Same trial. Very different feel.

visual.stat_label: Stayed on vs everyone counted, top dose

scenes.retention_device: Closes the loop on the exact numbers from the hook

scenes.section: How to read any GLP-1 headline
scenes.narration: Then add four quick follow-ups. Who was studied, with or without diabetes? For how long? Compared with placebo or another drug? And how many people stopped, and why?
scenes.retention_device: Practical takeaway checklist

scenes.section: How to read any GLP-1 headline
scenes.narration: Run any headline through those five, and an 'up to' number is far less likely to catch you off guard.

factcheck.summary:
I checked the main numbers against Healio's EASD/NEJM report, Boehringer's press release, Fierce Biotech, and Healio's TRIUMPH-2 report. All of them match.

**SYNCHRONIZE-2 (verified):**
- 752 adults, 76 weeks, two doses (3.6 and 6 mg) and placebo.
- Weight loss, counting everyone: 8.2% and 9.8% vs 3.9% on placebo. Counting only people who stayed on treatment: 13.1% on the 6 mg dose vs 3.1% on placebo.
- A1C fell 0.9 and 0.8 points vs 0.2 on placebo, from a starting average of 7.4%. The company's stayed-on-treatment figure is 1.21 vs 0.03.
- Gut side effects: 72.8% and 77.7% vs 38.6% on placebo.
- Stopped because of gut side effects: 18% and 17.9% vs 1.2% on placebo.

**Investor reaction (verified):** Fierce reported Zealand shares down 11% and a 26% rate of stopping after any side effect, with no placebo figure given.

**TRIUMPH-2 (verified):** 11.9%, 16.8% and 18.8% vs 5.1% on placebo at 80 weeks, counting everyone. Published in The Lancet around 30 September 2026.

**From established literature (not re-opened this run):** the STEP 1, STEP 2, SURMOUNT-1 and SURMOUNT-2 figures match the published trials. The script already explains the two ways of counting, gives a placebo figure next to every number, warns that the trials aren't head-to-head, hedges claims to October 2026, includes the prescriber line, and tells viewers not to buy survodutide online.

**Not opened:** the NEJM and Lancet journal pages blocked access (403), so I confirmed those two papers through reputable secondary reports.

Only minor wording fixes are needed.

issues.claim: newer drugs, including pills and triple-hormone medicines like retatrutide, are moving through the pipeline
issues.problem: An oral semaglutide pill for weight (Wegovy pill) was already FDA-approved in December 2025. 'Pills ... moving through the pipeline' suggests no GLP-1 weight pill is approved yet, so it's a bit imprecise.
issues.fix: Competition, because this space is crowded. Semaglutide and tirzepatide are already approved, and more drugs, including new pills like orforglipron and triple-hormone medicines like retatrutide, are moving through the pipeline.

issues.claim: In major trials of this drug class, people with type 2 diabetes lose less weight than people without it.
issues.problem: This compares separate trials, not people within one trial. As written it sounds like a measured comparison inside a study.
issues.fix: Here's a pattern that rarely makes the headlines. In major trials of this drug class, trials in people with type 2 diabetes report less weight loss than trials in people without it.

issues.problem: Boehringer's press release says 755 participants, while Healio's report of the paper says 752. Viewers may see both numbers.
issues.fix: 752 adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes were randomly assigned to weekly survodutide, at a 3.6 or 6.0 milligram trial dose, or to placebo. (Keep 752, the number in the paper's report. Optionally add the on-screen note 'Company release: 755 enrolled'.)

issues.claim: about 18% of people on survodutide stopped because of gut side effects
issues.problem: The per-arm figures are 18% (3.6 mg) and 17.9% (6 mg). 'About 18%' is accurate, but saying 'on either dose' makes it clear the figure covers both arms.
issues.fix: And more people stopped. About 18% of people on either survodutide dose stopped because of gut side effects, versus 1.2% on placebo. And reports covering the investor reaction focused on how many people stopped.

issues.problem: For a living web page, the year should be labelled as the last-reviewed date rather than shown as a publication year.
issues.fix: Set the year to the page's 'Content current as of' date and label it 'last reviewed'.

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are clean, on-brand, and legible, but #0 ('WHY SHARES FELL?') has the strongest emotional pull (a single shocked-face pill character, clear directional arrow) and the sharpest curiosity gap against the title: the title already shows a strong win over placebo (9.8% vs 3.9%), so 'why did shares fall anyway?' is a genuinely surprising, specific hook that the video is confirmed to pay off (investor reaction vs side-effect profile). It also reads fastest at phone size with only two short text blocks and one focal character. #1 ('THE CATCH?') is legible and clean but more generic/abstract (no face, no specific tease) so likely lower CTR. #2 ('WHO'S RIGHT?') is the most cluttered — two characters, a VS, two small pill-shaped badges (SHARES/TRIAL) — which splits the focal point and pushes legibility of the badge text close to the phone-size threshold. #0 best balances curiosity, emotion, and single-glance clarity without overstating the video's content.
